message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2026) Below is a concise overview of the key protections and responsibilities that apply to residential tenants in Texas. These rights are derived from state statutes (primarily the Texas Property Code), local ordinances, and general landlord‑tenant law. While this list is comprehensive, it is not exhaustive; you may want to consult a local attorney or tenant‑rights organization for specific situations. | Category | What You’re Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |----------|------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • The landlord may charge a **maximum of one month’s rent** for a security deposit.
• The deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a written lease and a copy of the deposit receipt.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions if the deposit is withheld. | | **Habitability** | • The landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control).
• The landlord must repair or replace broken fixtures, appliances, and structural elements. | • Notify the landlord in writing (email or certified mail) of needed repairs.
• If repairs are not made within a reasonable time, you may withhold rent, repair and deduct, or pursue a lawsuit. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease specifies them and they are **reasonable** (not punitive). | • Pay on time or negotiate a payment plan if you’re experiencing hardship. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • You have the right to live without unreasonable interference from the landlord or other tenants. | • Report any harassment, unlawful entry, or noise complaints to the landlord in writing. | | **Landlord Entry** | • Landlords must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of all entries. If the landlord enters without notice, you can refuse entry. | | **Privacy** | • The landlord cannot monitor your personal activities or read your mail. | • Report any violations to the landlord or local authorities. | | **Discrimination** | • Texas law (and federal Fair Housing Act) prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or other protected classes. | • File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party may terminate a lease with proper notice: **30 days** for month‑to‑month leases, or the notice period specified in a fixed‑term lease.
• Landlords must provide a **written notice** of termination. | • Keep copies of all notices. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major defect, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from your rent, provided you follow the proper procedure. | • Document the defect, notify the landlord, keep receipts, and calculate the deduction. | | **Rent Increase** | • For month‑to‑month leases, landlords can raise rent with **30 days’ notice**.
• For fixed‑term leases, rent increases are only allowed if the lease allows it or at the end of the term. | • Review your lease for any rent‑increase clauses. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the Texas **eviction procedure**: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for nonpayment, 30‑day notice for lease violation), file a lawsuit, and obtain a court order. | • Respond to notices promptly. If you believe the eviction is unlawful, file a defense in court. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify which utilities you are responsible for. | • Verify utility responsibilities in the lease and keep records of payments. | | **Insurance** | • Landlords are not required to provide renter’s insurance, but it is highly recommended. | • Obtain renter’s insurance to protect personal property and liability. | | **Maintenance of Common Areas** | • Landlords must maintain common areas (hallways, stairwells, elevators) in a safe condition. | • Report hazards to the landlord in writing. | | **Subletting** | • Subletting is allowed only if the lease permits it or the landlord consents. | • Get written permission before subletting. | | **Legal Remedies** | • If your rights are violated, you can:
1. File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights (for discrimination).
2. File a civil action in court for damages or injunctions.
3. Seek mediation or arbitration if the lease provides for it. | • Keep all documentation (emails, texts, photos, receipts). | --- #### Quick Tips for Protecting Your Rights 1. **Read the Lease Carefully** – All obligations and rights are spelled out in the lease. 2. **Document Everything** – Photos, videos, written notices, and receipts help build a record. 3. **Communicate in Writing** – Email or certified mail provides proof of notice. 4. **Know the Timeline** – Texas law sets specific notice periods for rent increases, repairs, and evictions. 5. **Seek Help Early** – If you’re facing a dispute, contact a local tenant‑rights group or legal aid clinic before the situation escalates. --- #### Useful Resources | Resource | What It Offers | |----------|----------------| | **Texas Commission on Human Rights** | File discrimination complaints. | | **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection** | Information on landlord‑tenant disputes. | | **Local Tenant‑Rights Organizations** | Free or low‑cost legal assistance. | | **HUD – Fair Housing** | National resources and complaint filing. | | **Texas Property Code** | Full statutory text (available online). | --- **Disclaimer:** This overview is for informational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. Laws can change, and local ordinances may add additional protections. For specific legal questions, consult a licensed attorney in Texas.
